t: Zigzag Grid Traversal With Skip — Simulation
o: Walk the grid row by row, alternating direction each row (right, then left, ...), and keep only every other visited cell. For [[1,2],[3,4]] the visit order is 1,2,3,4 and we keep 1,4; for [[2,1],[2,1],[2,1]] we keep 2,1,2; for [[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]] we keep 1,3,5,7,9. A boolean 'take' flag toggles on every visited cell regardless of direction, so reversing alternate rows before iterating keeps the logic direction-agnostic.
k: Reverse every odd-indexed row, then take every other element of the flattened sequence — the skip flag toggles globally, not per row.

a.i: Iterate rows; for odd rows traverse a reversed copy so the zigzag becomes a simple left-to-right scan. Maintain take = true and append a cell's value only when take is true, flipping take after every cell (taken or skipped).
s: For each row i, define seq = row if i is even else reversed row.
Append seq[k] to the result whenever the global take flag is true.
Flip take after each cell; return the result.
a.t: O(m*n) — every cell is examined exactly once.

w: The single global toggle is the whole trick — a common bug is resetting the flag at each row start, which produces wrong results whenever a row has odd length. Verify with the three samples, especially the 3x2 case where the parity carries across rows. Edge cases: odd-length rows shift the parity entering the next row (handled automatically by the global flag). Follow-up: skip every k-th cell, or traverse columns in zigzag instead.
